claims.text: Retention of toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by the stability and coherence of nanoscale phase boundaries.
Coherent nanoscale phase boundaries arrest crack propagation.
Segregation of a minor alloying element to boundaries enhances boundary cohesion.
Reducing the minor-element concentration weakens boundaries and causes a loss of toughness.
The proposed initial alloy has a balanced multiphase microstructure with coherent nanoscale phase boundaries and no intentional minor-element segregation.
The controlled intervention is to vary systematically the concentration of a boundary-segregating minor alloying element.
The compositional changes will remain within solubility limits to avoid macroscopically deleterious secondary phases.
Increasing the minor-element concentration enriches nanoscale chemically heterogeneous boundaries at grain interfaces.
The minor element preferentially segregates to grain boundaries.
Minor-element segregation increases grain-boundary cohesion and inhibits crack nucleation and propagation.
Stabilization of the boundary microstructure increases the alloy's capacity to absorb deformation energy.
Minor-element depletion reduces boundary cohesion and increases susceptibility to embrittlement.
An optimal increase in minor-element concentration will increase fracture toughness and impact-energy absorption relative to the baseline.
Reduced or no additional minor-element concentration will produce lower toughness and more brittle crack propagation relative to the baseline.
The baseline is a standard-composition high-entropy alloy without a controlled increase in the minor alloying element.
The proposed behavior holds only within a compositional window that permits boundary segregation without phase separation or brittle-intermetallic formation.
The proposed behavior is expected under operating temperatures and deformation conditions relevant to demanding engineering applications.

contradictions.description: The baseline is defined as having no controlled increase in the minor element, but the predicted outcome says an alloy with no additional minor element should lose toughness relative to that same baseline.
The governing interfaces shift between nanoscale phase boundaries and grain boundaries; these are not necessarily the same interfaces, and the hypothesis does not establish their equivalence.
